title: The 59-Second Film That Refuses to Die: New Bigfoot Doc Promises Answers
summary:
Fifty-nine years ago, two men walked into the Six Rivers National Forest in Northern California and came out with 59 seconds of film that would never stop haunting us. Roger Patterson and Robert Gimlin claimed they encountered a Sasquatch — a tall, hairy creature walking upright through the woods. Their footage, known as the Patterson-Gimlin film, became the most analyzed and debated piece of cryptid evidence in history. The creature in it even got a nickname: Patty.

Now, a new documentary called 'Capturing Bigfoot' is ready to blow the legend wide open. It premiered earlier this year at SXSW in Austin, Texas, to a sold-out crowd. The screening electrified Bigfoot enthusiasts with its revelations, but then the film vanished — no other festivals, no streaming, nothing. The filmmakers deliberately held it back to preserve the mystery of never-before-seen footage featured in the movie.

Why the secrecy? Director Marq Evans and producer Tamir Ardon wanted audiences to experience the surprises together, just like Roger Patterson did when he toured the country screening his original film. That 1967 footage effectively went viral before the internet existed and grossed over $5 million in today's dollars.

'Capturing Bigfoot' follows Patterson's pursuit of the creature and the people whose lives were changed by it. When a reel of 16mm film is discovered in a safe five decades later, the story takes a sharp turn. The documentary features interviews with key figures like Bob Heironimus, Bob Gimlin, Jeff Meldrum, and Bill Munns — plus Roger's own son, Clint Patterson, and Clint's mother, Patricia, who have never spoken publicly about it before.

Director Marq Evans said in a statement, 'That footage is one of the most recognizable images in the world, but the people behind it have privately carried its weight for almost sixty years. This film is their story; about family, loyalty, and the truths they've held onto or finally let go of.'

XYZ Films will release 'Capturing Bigfoot' in New York, Los Angeles, and other select cities on October 20 — National Bigfoot Day. It will also be available to rent or buy on Prime Video in the U.S. and Canada that same day. Theatrical screenings will have heightened security, with recording devices strictly prohibited. A companion podcast launches this week on YouTube, with bonus episodes on Patreon.

So after nearly six decades, will we finally get answers? Or just more questions? Either way, the mystery of Patty isn't going anywhere.
why_it_matters: This story is really about how evidence and belief travel: the Patterson-Gimlin film has survived six decades because it is blurry enough to argue about, and the new movie's deliberate secrecy shows how mystery itself has become a marketing tool. For students learning to weigh sources, 'we finally have answers' is a claim worth checking — especially when the people making it also control the footage.

background_read: The Patterson-Gimlin film was shot on October 20, 1967 beside Bluff Creek in the Six Rivers National Forest — the same date fans now mark as National Bigfoot Day, which is why the new documentary is released on that day.
The two men were Roger Patterson (an amateur Bigfoot researcher and former rodeo rider) and Robert Gimlin (his friend and travelling companion).

Long before the film, Native American traditions along the Pacific Northwest coast told of 'wild men' of the forest, and the modern word 'Bigfoot' spread after a California newspaper printed stories in 1958 about giant footprints found at a construction site.

Over the decades the footage has been studied by animation artists, film labs and anatomy professors such as Jeff Meldrum (a scientist at Idaho State University who examines the footprints said to belong to a large unknown ape), while Bob Heironimus (a man from Yakima, Washington) has publicly claimed since the 1990s that he wore a fur suit that day — a claim Gimlin and the Patterson family have always denied.

SXSW (South by Southwest — a big yearly film, music and technology festival in Austin, Texas) hosted the movie's premiere, and XYZ Films (an independent company that buys and releases movies) is handling the October rollout, which includes a companion podcast.

perspectives.description: For Bigfoot fans, this is a serious, respectfully made film with a huge payoff: interviews with Bob Gimlin, footprint researcher Jeff Meldrum and family members like Clint and Patricia Patterson who had never spoken on camera. They see the withheld footage as proof the filmmakers have something genuinely new, not just another rehash of a famous clip.

Skeptics point out that keeping the film out of festivals and off streaming until a paid release lets it promise revelations without anyone being able to check them. They also note that the strongest evidence — the original 16mm film — is still the same ambiguous footage examined for decades, and that a documentary is storytelling, not proof.

In this view the film matters less as evidence than as a durable modern myth: an image that resists resolution is exactly why it keeps being re-examined, re-parodied and re-released. The 1967 screening tour, the October 20 'National Bigfoot Day' release and the podcast all follow the same playbook of keeping the mystery circulating.

New tools — high-resolution scanning, digital stabilisation and AI image analysis — could finally give the footage a more objective test, and the new reel supposedly found in a safe gives researchers something fresh to examine. If that material holds up, the debate could shift from folklore to forensics; if it doesn't, the legend will simply keep going.
